tabs.title: Understanding Space
tabs.description: Think about the details in the text.

tabs.title: Think Like a Scientist
tabs.description: Use the ideas in a new situation.

questions.q: How is an asteroid different from a star?
choices: It is always bigger than Earth.
It cannot make its own light.
It cannot move around the Sun.
It is made of water.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says asteroids are not stars and do not make their own light.

questions.q: Why is it wrong to say that all asteroids are very small?
choices: All asteroids are the size of cars.
Asteroids only move at night.
Every asteroid is a dwarf planet.
Some asteroids are bigger than mountains.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph compares some asteroids to cars and others to mountains.

questions.q: What can a scientist learn by taking many pictures of a space rock?
choices: How its position changes in the sky.
What people think about stars.
How old the Sun is today.
Why a telescope has glass.
questions.explanation: The scientist takes pictures to watch where asteroids travel.

questions.q: Why does Ceres not look like many other asteroids?
choices: It has no path around the Sun.
It is brighter than every star.
It is round rather than potato-shaped.
It comes from Earth's oceans.
questions.explanation: Ceres is described as round, while many other asteroids look like potatoes.

questions.q: Why do scientists use very large telescopes?
choices: Asteroids move only inside museums.
Asteroids can be very far away.
The Moon has no light at all.
A telescope makes the Sun smaller.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two explains that telescopes help scientists see distant objects.

questions.q: What can happen to a small piece of rock before it reaches the ground?
choices: It can turn into a new star.
It can always become a moon.
It can stop the Earth moving.
It can burn up in the air.
questions.explanation: Many small space rocks burn in Earth's atmosphere before reaching the ground.

questions.q: A child finds a small dark rock at a space museum. What could it be?
choices: A meteorite from space.
The centre of the Sun.
A piece of Earth's atmosphere.
A new planet orbiting Earth.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three calls a piece of space rock that can be touched in a museum a meteorite.

questions.q: You want to learn where an asteroid will go next. What should you look at?
choices: The colour of the telescope.
The names of famous stars.
Its path around the Sun.
The weather on Earth yesterday.
questions.explanation: The orbit is the path asteroids follow around the Sun.

questions.q: Why can watching the sky be useful for people on Earth?
choices: It makes big asteroids disappear.
It keeps all clouds away.
It stops every rock from moving.
Scientists can learn about possible space-rock dangers.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph explains that watching the sky helps scientists learn and keep people safe.

questions.q: What is one way a student can begin learning about space?
choices: Try to touch the Sun.
Look at the night sky and ask questions.
Go into space without help.
Wait until an asteroid hits Earth.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph encourages readers to look at stars on a clear night and ask questions.
